newsitem.title: USA: SPX climbs on Dutch auction tender offer.
newsitem.headline: SPX climbs on Dutch auction tender offer.

text.p: Shares in SPX Corp rose 6-1/2 to 52-3/8 Thursday after the company said it would pay $48 to $56 per share for 2.7 million shares in a Dutch auction share repurchase tender offer.
"Today's rally is on the announcement of that buyback, but this is part of an ongoing strategy," said Barrington Research analyst Alexander Paris.

The Muskegon, Mich.-based maker of automotive tools and equipment said it would start the Dutch auction on April 11. It also said that it was taking several other steps as part of a new financial strategy.
The company also said it was eliminating its quarterly cash dividend and expected that future distributions would be made through share repurchases.
Smith Barney analyst David Garrity said the market reaction indicated that "investors are clearly not wedded to dividends."
He added, "As a result of this transaction, the firm is substantially reducing its cost of capital ... Even on a worst case basis, the transaction is accretive to earnings per share."

Outlining additional measures, SPX said its new strategy aligns its financial and capital policies with the "Economic Value Added" financial management system that has been the basis of its performance measurement and compensation systems since early 1996.

SPX said it completed a tender offer to purchase for cash all its outstanding 11-3/4 percent senior subordinated notes due 2002 ($128.4 million in principal amount) and eliminate certain restrictive covenants. SPX said it started the tender March 11 and tenders for $126.7 million of notes and consents to eliminate the covenants had occurred as of March 25.
Payment will be made on April 14, it said.
"Completion of this action eliminated restrictive covenants which, among other things, prevented the company from repurchasing its own shares," SPX said.

The company said it received a firm commitment for a $400 million unsecured line of credit on March 31. "The new credit facility will provide the company with less restrictive covenants and lower cost capital in support of its growth strategy, permit the "Dutch auction" ... provide immediate capacity for acquisitions and add sufficient working capital flexibility for the immediate future," SPX said.
The Dutch Auction, which begins Friday, expires May 8.
Company directors and management have indicated that they will not tender their shares in the Dutch auction, SPX said.
The company said it intends to use borrowings under its revolving credit facility to purchase the shares.
Following completion of the Dutch auction, the company said it was authorized to purchase up to 200,000 more shares through open market or privately negotiated transactions.
Regarding elimination of the quarterly cash dividend, SPX said it "believes that repurchasing shares is a superior method of distributing cash to shareholders."
The company also said it has established a target book debt-to-total-capital ratio of 50 percent.
"Immediately after the Dutch auction, the company's leverage will exceed the target, but management believes that it can achieve this ratio within three years," SPX said.
